canaries.carnival-spirit:
--- couple/no/first/port-heavy
cabin.verified: true
cabin.call: Put them on a lower or middle deck, toward the middle of the ship — calmest ride, and the middle of the ship is the shortest walk to most of it.
cabin.flag[0]: Midship on decks 5, 6 or 7. A deck is only a safe default if it has cabins above it AND cabins below it — plenty of cabins on the deck itself proves nothing. On this class that band is genuinely three decks wide — deck 4 beneath 5 is cabin territory, so 5 passes where it wouldn't on a hull with public space under it. Deck 8 is the one that fails: Lido sits directly above it on 9. Still run the vertical scan on the specific cabin rather than blessing everything on 5 to 7. Cabins sit on deck 1 and then decks 4 through 8 — decks 2 and 3 aren't cabin decks here. The Lido on 9 sits cleanly above deck 8 rather than carrying cabins itself, which is the opposite of the Conquest and Sunshine hulls and makes deck 8 the straightforward pool-overhead case. Deck 1 carries cabins and needs a check of what shares and sits above it: there's an aft galley and service zone on deck 1 itself, and deck 2 above is predominantly public space rather than cabins. That's the opposite of how I'd describe most hulls, and it's the useful shape here.
cabin.flag[1]: I'd steer them off a porthole room — it's the cheapest category and they've felt small to me. Check the actual square footage for the specific cabin before you rule it in or out.
cabin.flag[2]: The bottom deck is fine if they're on a budget — that's where the cheap interiors are, and low is generally kinder for motion, not harsher.
cabin.flag[3]: Deck 8 is the top cabin deck and the pool deck is directly above it, with no cabins in between to absorb anything. A client asking for a high deck is asking for the noisiest one on this ship — offer them midship on 6 or 7 instead and tell them why.
cabin.flag[4]: These are narrow hulls, built to the original Panama Canal locks. That's a real difference from the rest of the fleet, but I have no evidence it changes how the ship rides or how big the cabins are — so don't sell it as an advantage or warn about it as a drawback. It's context, not a recommendation.
cabin.flag[5]: The lower level of the Dancin' nightclub was reportedly replaced in this ship's 2025 refurbishment, so older warnings about a two-level club over the lower cabins are out of date here. Check the current plan rather than a review.
cabin.flag[6]: Check what's directly above and below the cabin, worst first: **The pool or Lido deck** (deck 9, directly over the deck 8 cabins — the clean overhead case on this class, since the pool deck carries no cabins of its own) — chairs scraping, cleaning, footsteps, music, deck parties, worst early morning. **A galley or service area** (an aft galley and service block on deck 1 itself, alongside the cabins there) — carts, equipment, dishes, overnight and early prep.
cabin.flag[7]: Keep them out of a connecting cabin. That door is a bonus when your own people are on the other side of it and a problem when it's strangers — check the deck plan before you confirm.
cabin.why: Midship is the sweet spot on any ship: least motion, most central. Even for good sailors it saves them a hike to dinner every night. One caveat that catches people on the biggest ships: midship does not automatically mean near a lift. Some hulls put all their elevator banks forward and aft, so the calmest cabin can also be the longest walk to a lift — where that's true, the elevator note on this card says so.
money.verified: true
money.call: Skip the blanket drink package here. It's a port-heavy run — they'll be off the ship most days, and it rarely earns back its cost.
money.flag[0]: CHEERS! is $83.94 per person per day bought in advance and $89.94 bought onboard, and both figures already include the 20% service charge — so the price you see is the price they pay. Every guest of drinking age in the stateroom has to buy it if one does. Worth saying plainly when a client is comparing against another line: some lines post the package before their gratuity and add it at checkout, so a lower-looking number can end up costing more.
money.flag[1]: Book specialty dining now, before they board. It's reservable pre-cruise through Cruise Manager, and times are first-come first-served, so lock in the nights that matter early. When the client can't get a table they blame you, not the ship.
money.flag[2]: Set the gratuity expectation up front. It's auto-added to the folio daily — around $17 per person, per day — and first-timers are always surprised by the bill at the end.
money.why: A drink package has to be consumed on the ship. When the itinerary pulls them ashore five days out of seven, the daily rate almost never breaks even. Sell it and they feel it was a waste — and they remember who suggested it.
traps.verified: true
traps.call: Not many traps on this booking — but don't confirm it before you've glanced at these.
traps.flag[0]: If you've booked a balcony, confirm the view isn't blocked. Carnival sells three obstructed categories on this class rather than hiding them: 4K interior with window, 7A balcony and 9A premium balcony. The cause is the lifeboats, tender boats and davits on Main Deck 4. Named examples from the published list include 9A cabins 5241 and 5243 and a large run of 7A cabins starting around 5142 to 5191 with more further aft — that list hasn't been imported here cabin-by-cabin, so read the category code on the specific cabin. Watch the 4K, 7A and 9A categories — 9A cabins 5241 and 5243 and a long 7A run from around 5142 to 5191 are the named examples. What's actually in the way matters here: lifeboats, tenders and their davits — this takes the view straight DOWN more than the view out, and the horizon is often still there. Someone who wants to sit with a book and see sea can be very happy in one of these at a lower price — describe it rather than writing it off. The deck plan doesn't always flag it, and an obstructed view is the first thing the client notices.
traps.flag[1]: Walk them through embarkation-day timing. Guests pick an Arrival Appointment during online check-in and need to turn up inside that window — anyone arriving early may be held until their assigned time. First-timers show up whenever, then wait in a two-hour line — a staggered check-in window is the easiest good impression you'll ever make.
traps.flag[2]: Neither BOLT nor SkyRide is on this class — those are the Excel and Vista ships. Don't let a client arrive expecting the rollercoaster or the sky ride.
traps.flag[3]: Green Thunder is on all four ships in this class, and it's the one worth naming to a family rather than saying "there's a thrill slide" — that way you can explain exactly which child can ride what.
traps.why: Experienced or not, these catch people on every sailing, because none of them show up clearly at the point of booking.
summary: I've got you two set for the Carnival Spirit. I'm booking you toward the middle of the ship so you're close to everything and get the smoothest ride. I'd skip the drink package on this one — you'll be off exploring most days, so it wouldn't pay off. I'll also lock in your specialty dining before you sail so you get the nights you want.

Aft is the engines: you feel the vibration back there and the room itself can shake, which is a different complaint from motion and catches the people who assumed a low cabin at the back would be fine. Lower is generally better for motion too — closer to the waterline, less of the ship swinging around you. Midship is where you avoid both at once.
money.verified: true
money.call: Skip the blanket drink package here. It's a port-heavy run — they'll be off the ship most days, and it rarely earns back its cost.
money.flag[0]: CHEERS! is $83.94 per person per day bought in advance and $89.94 bought onboard, and both figures already include the 20% service charge — so the price you see is the price they pay. Every guest of drinking age in the stateroom has to buy it if one does. Worth saying plainly when a client is comparing against another line: some lines post the package before their gratuity and add it at checkout, so a lower-looking number can end up costing more.
money.flag[1]: Book specialty dining now, before they board. It's reservable pre-cruise through Cruise Manager, and times are first-come first-served, so lock in the nights that matter early. When the client can't get a table they blame you, not the ship.
money.flag[2]: Set the gratuity expectation up front. It's auto-added to the folio daily — around $17 per person, per day — and first-timers are always surprised by the bill at the end.
money.why: A drink package has to be consumed on the ship. When the itinerary pulls them ashore five days out of seven, the daily rate almost never breaks even. Sell it and they feel it was a waste — and they remember who suggested it.
traps.verified: true
traps.call: Not many traps on this booking — but don't confirm it before you've glanced at these.
traps.flag[0]: If you've booked a balcony, confirm the view isn't blocked. Carnival sells three obstructed categories on this class rather than hiding them: 4K interior with window, 7A balcony and 9A premium balcony. The cause is the lifeboats, tender boats and davits on Main Deck 4. Named examples from the published list include 9A cabins 5241 and 5243 and a large run of 7A cabins starting around 5142 to 5191 with more further aft — that list hasn't been imported here cabin-by-cabin, so read the category code on the specific cabin. Watch the 4K, 7A and 9A categories — 9A cabins 5241 and 5243 and a long 7A run from around 5142 to 5191 are the named examples. What's actually in the way matters here: lifeboats, tenders and their davits — this takes the view straight DOWN more than the view out, and the horizon is often still there. Someone who wants to sit with a book and see sea can be very happy in one of these at a lower price — describe it rather than writing it off. The deck plan doesn't always flag it, and an obstructed view is the first thing the client notices.
traps.flag[1]: Walk them through embarkation-day timing. Guests pick an Arrival Appointment during online check-in and need to turn up inside that window — anyone arriving early may be held until their assigned time. First-timers show up whenever, then wait in a two-hour line — a staggered check-in window is the easiest good impression you'll ever make.
traps.flag[2]: Neither BOLT nor SkyRide is on this class — those are the Excel and Vista ships. Don't let a client arrive expecting the rollercoaster or the sky ride.
traps.flag[3]: Green Thunder is on all four ships in this class, and it's the one worth naming to a family rather than saying "there's a thrill slide" — that way you can explain exactly which child can ride what.
traps.why: Experienced or not, these catch people on every sailing, because none of them show up clearly at the point of booking.
summary: I've got you two set for the Carnival Spirit. I'm putting you on a lower deck toward the middle of the ship on purpose — that's the steadiest part of the ship, so seasickness shouldn't be an issue. I'd skip the drink package on this one — you'll be off exploring most days, so it wouldn't pay off. I'll also lock in your specialty dining before you sail so you get the nights you want.

cabin.flag[2]: Midship on decks 5, 6 or 7. A deck is only a safe default if it has cabins above it AND cabins below it — plenty of cabins on the deck itself proves nothing. It's context, not a recommendation.
cabin.flag[7]: The lower level of the Dancin' nightclub was reportedly replaced in this ship's 2025 refurbishment, so older warnings about a two-level club over the lower cabins are out of date here. Check the current plan rather than a review.
cabin.flag[8]: Check what's directly above and below the cabin, worst first: **The pool or Lido deck** (deck 9, directly over the deck 8 cabins — the clean overhead case on this class, since the pool deck carries no cabins of its own) — chairs scraping, cleaning, footsteps, music, deck parties, worst early morning. **A galley or service area** (an aft galley and service block on deck 1 itself, alongside the cabins there) — carts, equipment, dishes, overnight and early prep.
cabin.flag[9]: Keep them out of a connecting cabin. That door is a bonus when your own people are on the other side of it and a problem when it's strangers — check the deck plan before you confirm.
cabin.why: A ship pivots around its center, like a seesaw: the ends rise and fall the most, the middle barely moves. But the two ends are bad for different reasons. Forward is the pitch — that's the motion people picture. Aft is the engines: you feel the vibration back there and the room itself can shake, which is a different complaint from motion and catches the people who assumed a low cabin at the back would be fine. Lower is generally better for motion too — closer to the waterline, less of the ship swinging around you. Midship is where you avoid both at once.
money.verified: true
money.call: The drink package is worth it on this sailing. Lots of sea days means lots of bar time — what it takes to break even depends entirely on what they actually drink, so run it against their habits rather than a rule of thumb.
money.flag[0]: CHEERS! is $83.94 per person per day bought in advance and $89.94 bought onboard, and both figures already include the 20% service charge — so the price you see is the price they pay. Every guest of drinking age in the stateroom has to buy it if one does. Worth saying plainly when a client is comparing against another line: some lines post the package before their gratuity and add it at checkout, so a lower-looking number can end up costing more.
money.flag[1]: Book specialty dining now, before they board. It's reservable pre-cruise through Cruise Manager, and times are first-come first-served, so lock in the nights that matter early. When the client can't get a table they blame you, not the ship.
money.why: Drink packages only win when people are actually on the ship drinking. Sea-day itineraries keep them aboard, so the break-even is easy to clear. On a port-heavy run it's the opposite.
traps.verified: true
traps.call: Watch the walking. This is a big ship, and the distance from a far cabin to the theater or dining room is longer than anyone expects — it wears on older travelers by day three.
traps.flag[0]: Map their daily route before you book the cabin. A smaller hull with a single Lido deck, so much less of the Excel-class problem where dining is low and the pool is eight decks up — though that comparison is our inference from the layout rather than a sourced claim. Secondary sources report around fifteen lifts but nothing establishes a bank layout, and a count with no layout gives you no useful advice, so check the deck plan for the specific cabin and confirm scooter clearance against Carnival's accessible deck plan. A great-looking aft suite can mean a punishing walk to everything, every night.
traps.flag[1]: If you've booked a balcony, confirm the view isn't blocked. Carnival sells three obstructed categories on this class rather than hiding them: 4K interior with window, 7A balcony and 9A premium balcony. The cause is the lifeboats, tender boats and davits on Main Deck 4. Named examples from the published list include 9A cabins 5241 and 5243 and a large run of 7A cabins starting around 5142 to 5191 with more further aft — that list hasn't been imported here cabin-by-cabin, so read the category code on the specific cabin. Watch the 4K, 7A and 9A categories — 9A cabins 5241 and 5243 and a long 7A run from around 5142 to 5191 are the named examples. What's actually in the way matters here: lifeboats, tenders and their davits — this takes the view straight DOWN more than the view out, and the horizon is often still there. Someone who wants to sit with a book and see sea can be very happy in one of these at a lower price — describe it rather than writing it off. The deck plan doesn't always flag it, and an obstructed view is the first thing the client notices.
traps.flag[2]: Neither BOLT nor SkyRide is on this class — those are the Excel and Vista ships. Don't let a client arrive expecting the rollercoaster or the sky ride.
traps.flag[3]: Green Thunder is on all four ships in this class, and it's the one worth naming to a family rather than saying "there's a thrill slide" — that way you can explain exactly which child can ride what.
traps.why: Deck plans hide scale. On a vessel this size, 'aft' to 'midship dining' can be a quarter-mile each way. For a multigen group with anyone slower on their feet, cabin placement is really a mobility decision in disguise.
summary: I've got the group set for the Carnival Spirit. I'm putting you on a lower deck toward the middle of the ship on purpose — that's the steadiest part of the ship, so seasickness shouldn't be an issue. With this many sea days, the drink package is genuinely worth it, so I'll add it. I've picked the cabin with the walking in mind, so nobody's hiking the length of the ship to get to dinner. I'll also lock in your specialty dining before you sail so you get the nights you want.

traps.flag[0]: If you've booked a balcony, confirm the view isn't blocked. Carnival sells three obstructed categories on this class rather than hiding them: 4K interior with window, 7A balcony and 9A premium balcony. The cause is the lifeboats, tender boats and davits on Main Deck 4. Named examples from the published list include 9A cabins 5241 and 5243 and a large run of 7A cabins starting around 5142 to 5191 with more further aft — that list hasn't been imported here cabin-by-cabin, so read the category code on the specific cabin. Watch the 4K, 7A and 9A categories — 9A cabins 5241 and 5243 and a long 7A run from around 5142 to 5191 are the named examples. What's actually in the way matters here: lifeboats, tenders and their davits — this takes the view straight DOWN more than the view out, and the horizon is often still there. Someone who wants to sit with a book and see sea can be very happy in one of these at a lower price — describe it rather than writing it off. The deck plan doesn't always flag it, and an obstructed view is the first thing the client notices.
traps.flag[1]: Neither BOLT nor SkyRide is on this class — those are the Excel and Vista ships. Don't let a client arrive expecting the rollercoaster or the sky ride.
traps.flag[2]: Green Thunder is on all four ships in this class, and it's the one worth naming to a family rather than saying "there's a thrill slide" — that way you can explain exactly which child can ride what.
traps.why: Experienced or not, these catch people on every sailing, because none of them show up clearly at the point of booking.
summary: I've got you set for the Carnival Spirit. I'm booking you toward the middle of the ship so you're close to everything and get the smoothest ride. With this many sea days, the drink package is genuinely worth it, so I'll add it. I'll also lock in your specialty dining before you sail so you get the nights you want.
--- solo/yes/first/port-heavy
cabin.verified: true
cabin.call: This one matters here — book them on a lower or middle deck, toward the middle of the ship. Nothing high, nothing at either end. That's where the ship moves least.
cabin.flag[0]: They're prone to seasickness. Push hard for midship. Extreme forward is the one to rule out; extreme aft is a negative when there's comparable midship inventory, and more so if vibration also matters to them.
cabin.flag[1]: Lower decks are generally better for motion, not worse — closer to the waterline. The catch is vibration: a low cabin at the back can still pick up the propulsion, so "go low" isn't automatically the right call for a sensitive traveller.
cabin.flag[2]: Midship on decks 5, 6 or 7. A deck is only a safe default if it has cabins above it AND cabins below it — plenty of cabins on the deck itself proves nothing. On this class that band is genuinely three decks wide — deck 4 beneath 5 is cabin territory, so 5 passes where it wouldn't on a hull with public space under it. Deck 8 is the one that fails: Lido sits directly above it on 9. Still run the vertical scan on the specific cabin rather than blessing everything on 5 to 7. Cabins sit on deck 1 and then decks 4 through 8 — decks 2 and 3 aren't cabin decks here. The Lido on 9 sits cleanly above deck 8 rather than carrying cabins itself, which is the opposite of the Conquest and Sunshine hulls and makes deck 8 the straightforward pool-overhead case. Deck 1 carries cabins and needs a check of what shares and sits above it: there's an aft galley and service zone on deck 1 itself, and deck 2 above is predominantly public space rather than cabins. That's the opposite of how I'd describe most hulls, and it's the useful shape here.
cabin.flag[3]: I'd steer them off a porthole room — it's the cheapest category and they've felt small to me. Check the actual square footage for the specific cabin before you rule it in or out.
cabin.flag[4]: The bottom deck is fine if they're on a budget — that's where the cheap interiors are, and low is generally kinder for motion, not harsher.
cabin.flag[5]: Deck 8 is the top cabin deck and the pool deck is directly above it, with no cabins in between to absorb anything. A client asking for a high deck is asking for the noisiest one on this ship — offer them midship on 6 or 7 instead and tell them why.
cabin.flag[6]: These are narrow hulls, built to the original Panama Canal locks. That's a real difference from the rest of the fleet, but I have no evidence it changes how the ship rides or how big the cabins are — so don't sell it as an advantage or warn about it as a drawback. It's context, not a recommendation.
cabin.flag[7]: The lower level of the Dancin' nightclub was reportedly replaced in this ship's 2025 refurbishment, so older warnings about a two-level club over the lower cabins are out of date here. Check the current plan rather than a review.
cabin.flag[8]: Check what's directly above and below the cabin, worst first: **The pool or Lido deck** (deck 9, directly over the deck 8 cabins — the clean overhead case on this class, since the pool deck carries no cabins of its own) — chairs scraping, cleaning, footsteps, music, deck parties, worst early morning. **A galley or service area** (an aft galley and service block on deck 1 itself, alongside the cabins there) — carts, equipment, dishes, overnight and early prep.
cabin.flag[9]: Keep them out of a connecting cabin. That door is a bonus when your own people are on the other side of it and a problem when it's strangers — check the deck plan before you confirm.
cabin.why: A ship pivots around its center, like a seesaw: the ends rise and fall the most, the middle barely moves. But the two ends are bad for different reasons. Forward is the pitch — that's the motion people picture. Aft is the engines: you feel the vibration back there and the room itself can shake, which is a different complaint from motion and catches the people who assumed a low cabin at the back would be fine. Lower is generally better for motion too — closer to the waterline, less of the ship swinging around you. Midship is where you avoid both at once.
money.verified: true
money.call: Skip the blanket drink package here. It's a port-heavy run — they'll be off the ship most days, and it rarely earns back its cost.
money.flag[0]: CHEERS! is $83.94 per person per day bought in advance and $89.94 bought onboard, and both figures already include the 20% service charge — so the price you see is the price they pay. Every guest of drinking age in the stateroom has to buy it if one does. Worth saying plainly when a client is comparing against another line: some lines post the package before their gratuity and add it at checkout, so a lower-looking number can end up costing more.
money.flag[1]: Book specialty dining now, before they board. It's reservable pre-cruise through Cruise Manager, and times are first-come first-served, so lock in the nights that matter early. When the client can't get a table they blame you, not the ship.
money.flag[2]: Set the gratuity expectation up front. It's auto-added to the folio daily — around $17 per person, per day — and first-timers are always surprised by the bill at the end.
money.why: A drink package has to be consumed on the ship. When the itinerary pulls them ashore five days out of seven, the daily rate almost never breaks even. Sell it and they feel it was a waste — and they remember who suggested it.

cabin.flag[1]: The deck 7 balconies have a quirk that's worth explaining rather than avoiding, and it's the thing most likely to be mis-sold on this class. cabin.flag[2]: Ask about the hump cabins rather than avoiding them. cabin.flag[3]: This class is built for looking at things — three acres of glass, panoramic lifts on the outside of the hull, a two-level glass-walled dining room, a retractable roof over the Solarium. cabin.flag[4]: Aft-facing balconies are a FIT question rather than a quality one. cabin.flag[5]: Check what's directly above and below the cabin, worst first: **The pool or Lido deck** (the pool and Solarium on deck 11, over the whole of deck 10 — chair-scraping early is the standing complaint) — chairs scraping, cleaning, footsteps, music, deck parties, worst early morning. **The buffet or a large restaurant** (the buffet aft on 11, over the aft deck 10 cabins — the most-complained-about spot, though that's passenger judgment) — carts, chairs, cleaning, early breakfast setup. **A sports court or running track** (the sports court on 12 and the rock wall and mini-golf on 13, all well above the cabin decks) — bouncing balls, running, stomping, basketball through the day.
cabin.flag[6]: Keep them out of a connecting cabin. That door is a bonus when your own people are on the other side of it and a problem when it's strangers — check the deck plan before you confirm.
cabin.why: Midship is the sweet spot on any ship: least motion, most central. Even for good sailors it saves them a hike to dinner every night. money.verified: true
money.call: Skip the blanket drink package here. It's a port-heavy run — they'll be off the ship most days, and it rarely earns back its cost.
money.flag[0]: Two things before you price this. money.flag[1]: Book specialty dining now, before they board. traps.call: Not many traps on this booking — but don't confirm it before you've glanced at these.
traps.flag[0]: If you've booked a balcony, confirm the view isn't blocked. Two mechanisms here and they call for opposite advice. The first is the deck 7 lifeboat roof on the indented sections — it takes the downward view and leaves the horizon, so it's a disclosure, not a veto. traps.flag[1]: Walk them through embarkation-day timing. Turn up inside the window: early arrivals wait outside the terminal and late ones board with a later group. How hard it's enforced varies by port. First-timers show up whenever, then wait in a two-hour line — a staggered check-in window is the easiest good impression you'll ever make.
traps.flag[2]: This class is a SCENERY-FIRST Royal Caribbean product, not an attraction-first one, and that's the sentence to lead with rather than a list of what's missing. What isn't: FlowRider, ice rink, waterslides, bumper cars, North Star, Central Park or Boardwalk. traps.flag[3]: On the right itinerary these ships beat the big ones outright — Alaska, the Panama Canal, Europe. On a Caribbean sea-day run they don't. That's the single best matching question on this class, and it's an itinerary question rather than a ship one.

traps.linePolicy[1]: Voom Wi-Fi is priced per device per day, not per cabin — roughly $18 to $38 a day each, and materially cheaper pre-cruise. A family of four assuming one household plan is in for a real shock.
traps.linePolicy[2]: Room service is $7.95 per order plus 18%, so about $9.40 a delivery. Continental breakfast is still free.
traps.linePolicy[3]: The Key costs roughly $26 to $50 per person per day and every guest aged 6 and over in the stateroom has to buy it — the same all-or-nothing structure as the drink package.
traps.linePolicy[4]: One 750ml bottle of wine per drinking-age guest on embarkation day, and $15 corkage if they drink it anywhere public. Anything bought in port is held until the last night.

Aft is the engines: you feel the vibration back there and the room itself can shake, which is a different complaint from motion and catches the people who assumed a low cabin at the back would be fine. Lower is generally better for motion too — closer to the waterline, less of the ship swinging around you. Midship is where you avoid both at once.

money.flag[0]: Two things before you price this. traps.flag[0]: If you've booked a balcony, confirm the view isn't blocked. Two mechanisms here and they call for opposite advice. The first is the deck 7 lifeboat roof on the indented sections — it takes the downward view and leaves the horizon, so it's a disclosure, not a veto. The second is genuinely blocking and it's specific: 9252 and 9652 are obstructed by the ship's window-washing platform, and that pair holds across all four hulls, which is unusual enough to be worth knowing by cabin number. Structural obstructions are the ship-specific part. On this ship 7170 and 7670 are identified as partially blocked by the ship's own structure. A much broader claim circulates that a long run of deck 7 cabins is lifeboat-obstructed; it comes from a low-quality source and it confuses the roof issue with a blocked horizon, so read the current plan rather than believing it. traps.flag[1]: Walk them through embarkation-day timing. traps.flag[2]: This class is a SCENERY-FIRST Royal Caribbean product, not an attraction-first one, and that's the sentence to lead with rather than a list of what's missing. traps.flag[0]: If you've booked a balcony, confirm the view isn't blocked. Two mechanisms here and they call for opposite advice. The first is the deck 7 lifeboat roof on the indented sections — it takes the downward view and leaves the horizon, so it's a disclosure, not a veto. The second is genuinely blocking and it's specific: 9252 and 9652 are obstructed by the ship's window-washing platform, and that pair holds across all four hulls, which is unusual enough to be worth knowing by cabin number. Structural obstructions are the ship-specific part. On this ship 7170 and 7670 are identified as partially blocked by the ship's own structure. A much broader claim circulates that a long run of deck 7 cabins is lifeboat-obstructed; it comes from a low-quality source and it confuses the roof issue with a blocked horizon, so read the current plan rather than believing it. Watch cabins 9252 and 9652 on every hull in the class, blocked by the window-washing platform — plus the deck 7 lifeboat roof, which is a downward-view issue rather than a blocked one. What's actually in the way matters here: a structural roof or canopy covering the lifeboats BELOW the balcony, extending out from under it — the horizon and the sea out in front are essentially preserved — what's gone is the view straight down at the water. Disclose it and let them decide; this is not a reason to steer a scenic-view client away, and it only really matters to someone who pictured looking down from their own rail. And separately, the ship's window-washing platform and its equipment — an unusual one, and it affects a small number of specific cabins rather than a band — the platform sits in the view itself. Worth checking by cabin number rather than by deck, because the cabins either side can be perfectly clear. And separately, solid structure — a steel bulkhead, panel or railing — this is the kind that genuinely takes the view, and on some ships it blocks everything from a seated position and opens up when you stand. Steer a client who is buying the view somewhere else. The deck plan doesn't always flag it, and an obstructed view is the first thing the client notices.
traps.flag[1]: Walk them through embarkation-day timing. Check-in opens 45 days before sailing and arrival windows are picked then, in half-hour slots from about 10:30am to 2:30pm — first-come first-served, so the client who checks in on day 45 gets the early boarding and the one who waits gets 2pm. Turn up inside the window: early arrivals wait outside the terminal and late ones board with a later group. How hard it's enforced varies by port. First-timers show up whenever, then wait in a two-hour line — a staggered check-in window is the easiest good impression you'll ever make.
traps.flag[2]: This class is a SCENERY-FIRST Royal Caribbean product, not an attraction-first one, and that's the sentence to lead with rather than a list of what's missing. What's aboard: the rock wall, the nine-hole mini-golf course, the sports court, an arcade and Adventure Ocean. What isn't: FlowRider, ice rink, waterslides, bumper cars, North Star, Central Park or Boardwalk. A family who booked Royal Caribbean expecting the advertising will be disappointed by a ship that isn't trying to be that — so set the frame before they book, and sell the glass, the Solarium roof and the itinerary instead.
traps.flag[3]: On the right itinerary these ships beat the big ones outright — Alaska, the Panama Canal, Europe. On a Caribbean sea-day run they don't. That's the single best matching question on this class, and it's an itinerary question rather than a ship one.
traps.flag[4]: Don't repeat the claim that a long run of deck 7 cabins here is lifeboat-obstructed. The real deck 7 issue is a roof that blocks the view downward while leaving the horizon open, which is a different thing and a much smaller problem. Being able to correct that is worth a booking.
traps.why: Experienced or not, these catch people on every sailing, because none of them show up clearly at the point of booking.
traps.linePolicy[0]: From 15 March 2026 the Deluxe and Refreshment packages no longer include the Coca-Cola Freestyle cup — it's $4.99 onboard now. Only the Classic Soda package still includes it. Anyone who booked before that date was grandfathered, so a repeat client may be comparing against what they got last year.
traps.linePolicy[1]: Voom Wi-Fi is priced per device per day, not per cabin — roughly $18 to $38 a day each, and materially cheaper pre-cruise. A family of four assuming one household plan is in for a real shock.
traps.linePolicy[2]: Room service is $7.95 per order plus 18%, so about $9.40 a delivery. Continental breakfast is still free.
traps.linePolicy[3]: The Key costs roughly $26 to $50 per person per day and every guest aged 6 and over in the stateroom has to buy it — the same all-or-nothing structure as the drink package.
traps.linePolicy[4]: One 750ml bottle of wine per drinking-age guest on embarkation day, and $15 corkage if they drink it anywhere public. Anything bought in port is held until the last night.
traps.linePolicy[5]: Taxes, fees and port expenses sit outside the fare and vary by sailing. A free-cruise certificate never covers them, and that's a conversation to have before deposit rather than at final payment.
summary: I've got you set for the Radiance of the Seas. I'm booking you toward the middle of the ship so you're close to everything and get the smoothest ride. I'd skip the drink package on this one — you'll be off exploring most days, so it wouldn't pay off. I'll also lock in your specialty dining before you sail so you get the nights you want.
--- solo/no/first/sea-days
cabin.verified: true
cabin.call: Put them on a lower or middle deck, toward the middle of the ship — calmest ride, and the middle of the ship is the shortest walk to most of it.
cabin.flag[0]: Midship on decks 8 or 9. A deck is only a safe default if it has cabins above it AND cabins below it — plenty of cabins on the deck itself proves nothing. Here that lands on a narrow two-deck band and the working is worth knowing: cabins run 2 to 4 and then 7 to 10, so deck 7 fails BELOW — deck 6 under it is public space — and deck 10 fails ABOVE, with the pool, Solarium and Windjammer directly over it on 11. Everything in between is genuinely sandwiched. Every deck 10 cabin needs an overhead check rather than a blanket no: deck 11 above it is the pool, the Solarium and the Windjammer, so identify which venue actually sits over the specific cabin. For a light sleeper that's a strong negative. For someone who wants one deck's access to the pool and the buffet it can be a perfectly good trade. The aft end under the buffet is the most-complained-about spot, but that's passenger judgment rather than anything measured. The good news structurally is that the pool deck sits ABOVE the cabins rather than among them, which is the older and cleaner arrangement — below deck 10 you're between cabin decks the whole way.
cabin.flag[1]: The deck 7 balconies have a quirk that's worth explaining rather than avoiding, and it's the thing most likely to be mis-sold on this class. On the indented sections, a metal roof covering the lifeboats extends roughly eight to ten feet outward from below the balcony. What that costs you is the view STRAIGHT DOWN at the water. What it does not cost you is the horizon — the outward sea view stays substantially open. So disclose it and let them decide. Don't turn "can't look straight down" into "obstructed balcony", which is what the blogs do; a client who wants to sit with the sea in front of them will be perfectly happy here, often at a lower price.
cabin.flag[2]: Ask about the hump cabins rather than avoiding them. These sit on the outward bulge of the hull, which is where the deck 7 lifeboat-roof problem disappears and where the angled position gives better views both down and along the side of the ship. One thing not to promise: the balcony isn't necessarily bigger. Reports show hump cabins with ordinary-size balconies and excellent view geometry, which are different things. The specific hump cabin numbers for this hull need reading off its own plan — don't inherit another ship's.
cabin.flag[3]: This class is built for looking at things — three acres of glass, panoramic lifts on the outside of the hull, a two-level glass-walled dining room, a retractable roof over the Solarium. On an Alaska or Panama Canal itinerary that IS the product, and it beats the big ships outright. On a Caribbean sea-day run it doesn't.
cabin.flag[4]: Aft-facing balconies are a FIT question rather than a quality one. For a client on a scenic itinerary who wants wake views and long stretches of outdoor time, the view astern is the whole reason to be on this ship and the aft balcony is the cabin to push. For a client who's motion-sensitive, or slower on their feet, or who'll resent the corridor walk, it's the wrong room regardless of the view. Ask which one you have before you recommend it.
cabin.flag[5]: Check what's directly above and below the cabin, worst first: **The pool or Lido deck** (the pool and Solarium on deck 11, over the whole of deck 10 — chair-scraping early is the standing complaint) — chairs scraping, cleaning, footsteps, music, deck parties, worst early morning. **The buffet or a large restaurant** (the buffet aft on 11, over the aft deck 10 cabins — the most-complained-about spot, though that's passenger judgment) — carts, chairs, cleaning, early breakfast setup. **A sports court or running track** (the sports court on 12 and the rock wall and mini-golf on 13, all well above the cabin decks) — bouncing balls, running, stomping, basketball through the day.
cabin.flag[6]: Keep them out of a connecting cabin. That door is a bonus when your own people are on the other side of it and a problem when it's strangers — check the deck plan before you confirm.
cabin.why: Midship is the sweet spot on any ship: least motion, most central. Even for good sailors it saves them a hike to dinner every night. One caveat that catches people on the biggest ships: midship does not automatically mean near a lift. Some hulls put all their elevator banks forward and aft, so the calmest cabin can also be the longest walk to a lift — where that's true, the elevator note on this card says so.
money.verified: true
money.call: The drink package is worth it on this sailing. Lots of sea days means lots of bar time — what it takes to break even depends entirely on what they actually drink, so run it against their habits rather than a rule of thumb.
money.flag[0]: Two things before you price this. The 18% gratuity is added at checkout rather than included, so the real daily cost is about a fifth above the headline — and if one adult in the stateroom buys the alcohol package, every guest of drinking age in that stateroom has to buy it too. For a couple where only one drinks, that doubles the bill. The non-alcoholic packages can be bought individually, so that's the way round it.
money.flag[1]: Book specialty dining now, before they board. Book it in the Cruise Planner before you sail — reservations close about two days out, and the dining-package holders all book their times onboard, so the 6:30 to 8:00 slots and the sea-day nights go first. When the client can't get a table they blame you, not the ship.
money.flag[2]: Set the gratuity expectation up front. It's auto-added to the folio daily — around $18.50 per person, per day — and first-timers are always surprised by the bill at the end.
money.why: Drink packages only win when people are actually on the ship drinking. Sea-day itineraries keep them aboard, so the break-even is easy to clear. On a port-heavy run it's the opposite.

traps.flag[0]: If you've booked a balcony, confirm the view isn't blocked. The documented issue on this class is not a blocked view at all — it's the slide structure running down the hull past the balconies between decks 8 and 16, entering the balcony on some cabins. Treat that as a geometry check on the specific room. Beyond it, NCL doesn't publish a full obstructed list and says so obliquely in its own guarantee terms, which warn that a guarantee balcony may be fully or partially obstructed. Lists of specific cabin numbers circulate, but they come from a single site that concedes in the same article that NCL doesn't flag most of them, so none of those numbers are repeated here. What's actually in the way matters here: the ship's dry-slide structure running down the side of the hull, physically entering the balcony — this one is not a view problem and calling it "obstructed" misses it entirely — the client still has a balcony and the sea is still there, but the slide structure comes INTO the balcony space rather than passing outside it. The rooms with the biggest balconies are the ones reported worst affected, which is the opposite of what anyone expects. Describe the geometry; don't file it under obstructed and let them imagine a wall. The deck plan doesn't always flag it, and an obstructed view is the first thing the client notices.
traps.flag[1]: Walk them through embarkation-day timing. Check-in opens 21 days before sailing, not the 45 Royal gives you, and has to be done at least 3 days out. The arrival window is picked during check-in, and there's a security selfie to upload as part of it — worth warning a less tech-comfortable client about in advance, because eDocs are needed to get onto the pier at all. First-timers show up whenever, then wait in a two-hour line — a staggered check-in window is the easiest good impression you'll ever make.
traps.flag[2]: Nothing sits underneath the go-kart track. The Speedway runs across decks 18 to 20 and what's directly below it is the deck 17 pool deck, not staterooms — the nearest cabins are two decks further down. If a client has been warned off this ship over kart noise in the cabin, the deck plan doesn't support it, and correcting that is worth as much as finding a bad cabin.
traps.flag[3]: Ocean Boulevard, the wraparound promenade on deck 8, has no cabins on it. This is NOT Royal Promenade geometry — there's no corridor of stateroom windows looking onto a public walkway, so none of the privacy problems you'd warn about on those ships apply here. From a balcony above you can see down onto the promenade but not into the balconies either side.
traps.why: Experienced or not, these catch people on every sailing, because none of them show up clearly at the point of booking.
traps.linePolicy[0]: Be precise about The Haven, because two different mistakes cost bookings. First: a Club Balcony Suite is not a Haven category and carries the lower service charge — selling "a suite" is not selling Haven access. Second: the Haven is not the same product ship to ship. The newest hulls have the full complex with its own restaurant, pool and sundeck; the oldest have a small enclave and no Haven restaurant at all. Check what this specific ship's Haven actually includes before you describe it.
traps.linePolicy[1]: Freestyle means no assigned table and no fixed dinner time, which is the selling point — but it also means everyone turns up at once. The 6:30 to 7:30 window fills hard on the bigger ships and queueing is routine. Tell them to eat at 5:30 or after 8, or to book ahead even where it isn't required. The ships show colour-coded capacity boards for each venue; a red bar means don't walk over.
traps.linePolicy[2]: Prepaid service charges do not cover bar, beverage or specialty-dining gratuities. That one sentence causes more onboard disputes than anything else on this line — say it at final payment.
traps.linePolicy[3]: Free at Sea Plus is $49.99 per person per day, applies to guests one and two, and every guest in the stateroom has to take the same offer. It has to be added at least 72 hours before sailing and can't be changed onboard, so it's a pre-cruise decision or it's nothing.
traps.linePolicy[4]: Drinks at Great Stirrup Cay, the private island, are carved out of standard Free at Sea and sold as a separate island package. Free at Sea Plus covers them; the standard bundle doesn't. Clients assume the private island is included and it isn't.
traps.linePolicy[5]: Wi-Fi is per device per day — around $30 for browsing and $40 for streaming. A couple with two phones each is paying four times what they think they are.
traps.linePolicy[6]: Room service carries a convenience fee per order, about $5 at breakfast and up to $10 the rest of the day. It's waived in suites and The Haven, so a client moving down from a suite next time will notice.
summary: I've got you two set for the Norwegian Prima. I'm booking you toward the middle of the ship so you're close to everything and get the smoothest ride. I'd skip the drink package on this one — you'll be off exploring most days, so it wouldn't pay off. I'll also lock in your specialty dining before you sail so you get the nights you want.
--- couple/no/first/sea-days
cabin.verified: true
cabin.call: Put them on a lower or middle deck, toward the middle of the ship — calmest ride, and the middle of the ship is the shortest walk to most of it.
cabin.flag[0]: Midship on decks 10 to 13. A deck is only a safe default if it has cabins above it AND cabins below it — plenty of cabins on the deck itself proves nothing. Cabins run from 9 up to 16 here, and 10 to 13 is the strongest contiguous cabin-heavy band — NCL's own inventory puts the solo Studios midship on 12 and 13, which tells you something about where the quiet middle of this ship is. Deck 9 needs the check below it, because the forward end sits over the theatre. From 14 up, check what's overhead on the specific cabin rather than trusting the band. And let the actual vertical scan override the default: this is a starting point, not a verdict. Deck 16 is the top of the cabin range and the pool deck and the Surfside Café sit directly on 17 above it — a strong negative for a light sleeper and a reasonable trade for someone who wants the pool one flight up. Ask which client you have. Deck 8 is Ocean Boulevard — the wraparound outdoor promenade — and it carries no cabins at all, so nobody is living on it.
cabin.flag[1]: The most important check on this class, and it isn't what anyone expects. The Drop and The Rush run from deck 18 down to a terminus on deck 8, passing the balconies on the way — and on some cabins the slide structure comes INTO the balcony rather than passing outside it. Don't file that under "obstructed view", because the view is fine; what's gone is balcony space. The rooms with the LARGEST balconies are the ones reported worst affected, which is backwards from every instinct, so check the specific cabin against the deck plan before you confirm a family in a big-balcony category. This came from someone who sailed the ship and photographed it, which is why it's here at all — and the exact affected cabin numbers are not, because those need mapping from the geometry rather than guessing.
cabin.flag[2]: The solo Studios are a genuine reason to put a single client on this class. They're midship on decks 12 and 13 at about 94 to 95 square feet, with keycard access to a private Studio Lounge, and NCL's own words are that no single supplement is required — so you can say that plainly here rather than hedging it. They're small, and for the right solo traveller that's a trade worth making. I'm not giving you a count: sources differ wildly, so check live availability.
cabin.flag[3]: Club Balcony Suite is not a suite. It's a balcony stateroom with perks — earlier dining booking, an amenity, a laundry bag — with no suite-level access to anything, and it sits in the LOWER service-charge band. Clients hear "suite" and picture The Haven; be explicit that it isn't, especially with anyone coming from another line.
cabin.flag[4]: Don't quote a balcony size for this class from memory or from the launch campaign. NCL's own category pages show the dimensions varying substantially — an aft-facing balcony is far larger than a standard one — so read the figure for the specific ship and category. What is fair to say is that the cabin is genuinely big and the balcony is more ordinary than the advertising implied.
cabin.flag[5]: NCL's own guarantee language warns that an assigned guarantee balcony may be fully or partially obstructed. That's the line saying in its own terms that a guarantee category does not protect the view — so if the client cares about what they'll see, pick the cabin rather than taking the guarantee rate.
cabin.flag[6]: Check what's directly above and below the cabin, worst first: **The pool or Lido deck** (the pool deck on 17, directly over the deck 16 cabins — chair setup early is the standing complaint) — chairs scraping, cleaning, footsteps, music, deck parties, worst early morning. **The buffet or a large restaurant** (the Surfside Café, also on deck 17 above the same cabins) — carts, chairs, cleaning, early breakfast setup. **A kids' or water-play area** (Splash Academy on deck 15, which is itself a cabin deck — so it's a corridor check there rather than an overhead one) — running, activity noise, daytime traffic. **The theater or a show venue** (the theatre spans decks 6 to 8 forward and turns into a nightclub at night — the forward cabins on deck 9 are the ones above it) — bass, rehearsals, shows, mostly at night, with the odd daytime rehearsal.
cabin.flag[7]: Keep them out of a connecting cabin. That door is a bonus when your own people are on the other side of it and a problem when it's strangers — check the deck plan before you confirm.
cabin.why: Midship is the sweet spot on any ship: least motion, most central. Even for good sailors it saves them a hike to dinner every night. One caveat that catches people on the biggest ships: midship does not automatically mean near a lift. Some hulls put all their elevator banks forward and aft, so the calmest cabin can also be the longest walk to a lift — where that's true, the elevator note on this card says so.
money.verified: true
money.call: The drink package is worth it on this sailing. Lots of sea days means lots of bar time — what it takes to break even depends entirely on what they actually drink, so run it against their habits rather than a rule of thumb.
money.flag[0]: Do not tell an NCL client their drinks are free. Free at Sea bundles the open bar in, but it carries a mandatory fixed charge for every guest 21 and over — about $28.50 per person per day on sailings of six nights or more, and $32 on two-to-five-night sailings since May 2026 — and that STACKS on top of the ordinary daily service charge rather than replacing it. A Haven couple on a week is around $53.50 each per day before they buy a thing. Two more catches: the specialty dining in the bundle goes to guests one and two only, and a second guest under 21 gets a soda package at $12.50 a day charged separately, while guests three and up under 21 get no substitute at all.
money.flag[1]: Book specialty dining now, before they board. Book at 120 days out, the moment it opens — and know you're already behind. Suites, Club Balcony and the top Latitudes tiers get in at 125 days and clear the 6:30 to 8:00 slots at Cagney's, Le Bistro and Ocean Blue before general booking even starts. Take 5:30 or 9:00 rather than nothing, and warn them the "free" dinner still surcharges lobster and the premium steak cuts, with a second main at $25. When the client can't get a table they blame you, not the ship.
money.flag[2]: Set the gratuity expectation up front. It's auto-added to the folio daily — around $20 per person, per day — and first-timers are always surprised by the bill at the end.
money.why: Drink packages only win when people are actually on the ship drinking. Sea-day itineraries keep them aboard, so the break-even is easy to clear. On a port-heavy run it's the opposite.

cabin.call: This one matters here — book them on a lower or middle deck, toward the middle of the ship. Nothing high, nothing at either end. That's where the ship moves least.
cabin.flag[0]: They're prone to seasickness. Push hard for midship. Extreme forward is the one to rule out; extreme aft is a negative when there's comparable midship inventory, and more so if vibration also matters to them. I found nothing documented about how these specific hulls ride, so that's the general rule rather than a claim about these ships.
cabin.flag[1]: Lower decks are generally better for motion, not worse — closer to the waterline. The catch is vibration: a low cabin at the back can still pick up the propulsion, so "go low" isn't automatically the right call for a sensitive traveller.
cabin.flag[2]: Midship on decks 10 to 13. A deck is only a safe default if it has cabins above it AND cabins below it — plenty of cabins on the deck itself proves nothing. Cabins run from 9 up to 16 here, and 10 to 13 is the strongest contiguous cabin-heavy band — NCL's own inventory puts the solo Studios midship on 12 and 13, which tells you something about where the quiet middle of this ship is. Deck 9 needs the check below it, because the forward end sits over the theatre. From 14 up, check what's overhead on the specific cabin rather than trusting the band. And let the actual vertical scan override the default: this is a starting point, not a verdict. Deck 16 is the top of the cabin range and the pool deck and the Surfside Café sit directly on 17 above it — a strong negative for a light sleeper and a reasonable trade for someone who wants the pool one flight up. Ask which client you have. Deck 8 is Ocean Boulevard — the wraparound outdoor promenade — and it carries no cabins at all, so nobody is living on it.
cabin.flag[3]: The most important check on this class, and it isn't what anyone expects. The Drop and The Rush run from deck 18 down to a terminus on deck 8, passing the balconies on the way — and on some cabins the slide structure comes INTO the balcony rather than passing outside it. Don't file that under "obstructed view", because the view is fine; what's gone is balcony space. The rooms with the LARGEST balconies are the ones reported worst affected, which is backwards from every instinct, so check the specific cabin against the deck plan before you confirm a family in a big-balcony category. This came from someone who sailed the ship and photographed it, which is why it's here at all — and the exact affected cabin numbers are not, because those need mapping from the geometry rather than guessing.
cabin.flag[4]: The solo Studios are a genuine reason to put a single client on this class. They're midship on decks 12 and 13 at about 94 to 95 square feet, with keycard access to a private Studio Lounge, and NCL's own words are that no single supplement is required — so you can say that plainly here rather than hedging it. They're small, and for the right solo traveller that's a trade worth making. I'm not giving you a count: sources differ wildly, so check live availability.
cabin.flag[5]: Club Balcony Suite is not a suite. It's a balcony stateroom with perks — earlier dining booking, an amenity, a laundry bag — with no suite-level access to anything, and it sits in the LOWER service-charge band. Clients hear "suite" and picture The Haven; be explicit that it isn't, especially with anyone coming from another line.
cabin.flag[6]: Don't quote a balcony size for this class from memory or from the launch campaign. NCL's own category pages show the dimensions varying substantially — an aft-facing balcony is far larger than a standard one — so read the figure for the specific ship and category. What is fair to say is that the cabin is genuinely big and the balcony is more ordinary than the advertising implied.
cabin.flag[7]: NCL's own guarantee language warns that an assigned guarantee balcony may be fully or partially obstructed. That's the line saying in its own terms that a guarantee category does not protect the view — so if the client cares about what they'll see, pick the cabin rather than taking the guarantee rate.
cabin.flag[8]: Check what's directly above and below the cabin, worst first: **The pool or Lido deck** (the pool deck on 17, directly over the deck 16 cabins — chair setup early is the standing complaint) — chairs scraping, cleaning, footsteps, music, deck parties, worst early morning. **The buffet or a large restaurant** (the Surfside Café, also on deck 17 above the same cabins) — carts, chairs, cleaning, early breakfast setup. **A kids' or water-play area** (Splash Academy on deck 15, which is itself a cabin deck — so it's a corridor check there rather than an overhead one) — running, activity noise, daytime traffic. **The theater or a show venue** (the theatre spans decks 6 to 8 forward and turns into a nightclub at night — the forward cabins on deck 9 are the ones above it) — bass, rehearsals, shows, mostly at night, with the odd daytime rehearsal.
cabin.flag[9]: Connecting cabins are the right call here — but never infer it from the category or from two cabin numbers sitting next to each other. Only an explicit connecting pair counts. Never read connecting status off the category or off two cabin numbers being next to each other — only an explicit connecting pair counts. Connecting cabins exist on this class but I couldn't find any published inventory, so treat it as something to confirm rather than assume.
cabin.flag[10]: On any itinerary touching a US, Canadian or Chinese port, a guest under 21 has to be with someone 21 or over in the same stateroom, a connecting one, or one directly side-by-side. Across the hallway does NOT count here — Royal Caribbean allows that and Norwegian explicitly doesn't, so don't carry the habit across. Guardian minimum is 21, which is looser than Carnival's 25, but the geometry is tighter than both. A guardian who isn't the parent needs a notarised consent letter at the pier.
cabin.why: A ship pivots around its center, like a seesaw: the ends rise and fall the most, the middle barely moves. But the two ends are bad for different reasons. Forward is the pitch — that's the motion people picture. Aft is the engines: you feel the vibration back there and the room itself can shake, which is a different complaint from motion and catches the people who assumed a low cabin at the back would be fine. Lower is generally better for motion too — closer to the waterline, less of the ship swinging around you. Midship is where you avoid both at once.
money.verified: true
money.call: The drink package is worth it on this sailing. Lots of sea days means lots of bar time — what it takes to break even depends entirely on what they actually drink, so run it against their habits rather than a rule of thumb.
money.flag[0]: Do not tell an NCL client their drinks are free. Free at Sea bundles the open bar in, but it carries a mandatory fixed charge for every guest 21 and over — about $28.50 per person per day on sailings of six nights or more, and $32 on two-to-five-night sailings since May 2026 — and that STACKS on top of the ordinary daily service charge rather than replacing it. A Haven couple on a week is around $53.50 each per day before they buy a thing. Two more catches: the specialty dining in the bundle goes to guests one and two only, and a second guest under 21 gets a soda package at $12.50 a day charged separately, while guests three and up under 21 get no substitute at all.
money.flag[1]: Book specialty dining now, before they board. Book at 120 days out, the moment it opens — and know you're already behind. Suites, Club Balcony and the top Latitudes tiers get in at 125 days and clear the 6:30 to 8:00 slots at Cagney's, Le Bistro and Ocean Blue before general booking even starts. Take 5:30 or 9:00 rather than nothing, and warn them the "free" dinner still surcharges lobster and the premium steak cuts, with a second main at $25. When the client can't get a table they blame you, not the ship.
money.flag[2]: Set the gratuity expectation up front. It's auto-added to the folio daily — around $20 per person, per day — and first-timers are always surprised by the bill at the end.
money.why: Drink packages only win when people are actually on the ship drinking. Sea-day itineraries keep them aboard, so the break-even is easy to clear. On a port-heavy run it's the opposite.
traps.verified: true
traps.call: Kid access is the trap on this ship. What the parents picture and what their kids can actually use are two different things — and nobody finds out until day one.
traps.flag[0]: Confirm the kids clear the height and age lines **before** you promise anything. On this ship specifically: the Speedway go-karts need 55 inches minimum and cap at 82 inches maximum — it's a height WINDOW, not just a floor, so a tall teenager can be turned away too. NCL's pages have carried different weight caps in different locales; the figure seen in August 2026 was 265 pounds, so quote it as approximate and confirm for the sailing. Closed flat shoes only — no Crocs and no flip-flops, which is the thing that actually sends families back to the cabin; The Drop, the free-fall slide, needs 55 inches and caps at 330 pounds; and The Rush needs 48 inches and caps at 330 pounds. Different rides, different numbers — clearing one does not clear the rest, so check the ride the child actually wants. Splash Academy runs Turtles 3–5, Seals 6–9 and Dolphins 10–12, with Entourage for teens 13–17. Guppies covers 6 months to 2 years but it's a parent-participation play session, not drop-off childcare — don't let a couple plan an evening around it. Core programming is free; the Late Night Fun Zone is $10 an hour per child. Registration is a one-time form per child, done on embarkation day. A tall six-year-old still gets turned away at the slide.
traps.flag[1]: If you've booked a balcony, confirm the view isn't blocked. The documented issue on this class is not a blocked view at all — it's the slide structure running down the hull past the balconies between decks 8 and 16, entering the balcony on some cabins. Treat that as a geometry check on the specific room. Beyond it, NCL doesn't publish a full obstructed list and says so obliquely in its own guarantee terms, which warn that a guarantee balcony may be fully or partially obstructed. Lists of specific cabin numbers circulate, but they come from a single site that concedes in the same article that NCL doesn't flag most of them, so none of those numbers are repeated here. What's actually in the way matters here: the ship's dry-slide structure running down the side of the hull, physically entering the balcony — this one is not a view problem and calling it "obstructed" misses it entirely — the client still has a balcony and the sea is still there, but the slide structure comes INTO the balcony space rather than passing outside it. The rooms with the biggest balconies are the ones reported worst affected, which is the opposite of what anyone expects. Describe the geometry; don't file it under obstructed and let them imagine a wall. The deck plan doesn't always flag it, and an obstructed view is the first thing the client notices.
traps.flag[2]: Walk them through embarkation-day timing. Check-in opens 21 days before sailing, not the 45 Royal gives you, and has to be done at least 3 days out. The arrival window is picked during check-in, and there's a security selfie to upload as part of it — worth warning a less tech-comfortable client about in advance, because eDocs are needed to get onto the pier at all. First-timers show up whenever, then wait in a two-hour line — a staggered check-in window is the easiest good impression you'll ever make.
traps.flag[3]: Nothing sits underneath the go-kart track. The Speedway runs across decks 18 to 20 and what's directly below it is the deck 17 pool deck, not staterooms — the nearest cabins are two decks further down. If a client has been warned off this ship over kart noise in the cabin, the deck plan doesn't support it, and correcting that is worth as much as finding a bad cabin.
traps.flag[4]: Ocean Boulevard, the wraparound promenade on deck 8, has no cabins on it. This is NOT Royal Promenade geometry — there's no corridor of stateroom windows looking onto a public walkway, so none of the privacy problems you'd warn about on those ships apply here. From a balcony above you can see down onto the promenade but not into the balconies either side.
traps.why: Every line splits kids' programming and thrill rides by age and height, and the cutoffs aren't on the booking page. A parent who was promised the waterpark and gets a crying kid at the rope is a parent who books with someone else next year.
traps.linePolicy[0]: Be precise about The Haven, because two different mistakes cost bookings. First: a Club Balcony Suite is not a Haven category and carries the lower service charge — selling "a suite" is not selling Haven access. Second: the Haven is not the same product ship to ship. The newest hulls have the full complex with its own restaurant, pool and sundeck; the oldest have a small enclave and no Haven restaurant at all. Check what this specific ship's Haven actually includes before you describe it.
traps.linePolicy[1]: Freestyle means no assigned table and no fixed dinner time, which is the selling point — but it also means everyone turns up at once. The 6:30 to 7:30 window fills hard on the bigger ships and queueing is routine. Tell them to eat at 5:30 or after 8, or to book ahead even where it isn't required. The ships show colour-coded capacity boards for each venue; a red bar means don't walk over.
traps.linePolicy[2]: Prepaid service charges do not cover bar, beverage or specialty-dining gratuities. That one sentence causes more onboard disputes than anything else on this line — say it at final payment.
traps.linePolicy[3]: Free at Sea Plus is $49.99 per person per day, applies to guests one and two, and every guest in the stateroom has to take the same offer. It has to be added at least 72 hours before sailing and can't be changed onboard, so it's a pre-cruise decision or it's nothing.
traps.linePolicy[4]: Drinks at Great Stirrup Cay, the private island, are carved out of standard Free at Sea and sold as a separate island package. Free at Sea Plus covers them; the standard bundle doesn't. Clients assume the private island is included and it isn't.
traps.linePolicy[5]: Wi-Fi is per device per day — around $30 for browsing and $40 for streaming. A couple with two phones each is paying four times what they think they are.
traps.linePolicy[6]: Room service carries a convenience fee per order, about $5 at breakfast and up to $10 the rest of the day. It's waived in suites and The Haven, so a client moving down from a suite next time will notice.
summary: I've got your crew set for the Norwegian Prima. I'm putting you on a lower deck toward the middle of the ship on purpose — that's the steadiest part of the ship, so seasickness shouldn't be an issue. With this many sea days, the drink package is genuinely worth it, so I'll add it. I'm double-checking the kids clear the height and age rules for the slides and clubs so there are no surprises on day one. I'll also lock in your specialty dining before you sail so you get the nights you want.

cabin.flag[9]: Connecting cabins are the right call here — but never infer it from the category or from two cabin numbers sitting next to each other. Only an explicit connecting pair counts. cabin.why: A ship pivots around its center, like a seesaw: the ends rise and fall the most, the middle barely moves. But the two ends are bad for different reasons. Forward is the pitch — that's the motion people picture. Aft is the engines: you feel the vibration back there and the room itself can shake, which is a different complaint from motion and catches the people who assumed a low cabin at the back would be fine. Lower is generally better for motion too — closer to the waterline, less of the ship swinging around you. Midship is where you avoid both at once.

traps.call: Kid access is the trap on this ship. What the parents picture and what their kids can actually use are two different things — and nobody finds out until day one.
traps.flag[0]: Confirm the kids clear the height and age lines **before** you promise anything. On this ship specifically: the Speedway go-karts need 55 inches minimum and cap at 82 inches maximum — it's a height WINDOW, not just a floor, so a tall teenager can be turned away too. NCL's pages have carried different weight caps in different locales; the figure seen in August 2026 was 265 pounds, so quote it as approximate and confirm for the sailing. Closed flat shoes only — no Crocs and no flip-flops, which is the thing that actually sends families back to the cabin; The Drop, the free-fall slide, needs 55 inches and caps at 330 pounds; and The Rush needs 48 inches and caps at 330 pounds. Different rides, different numbers — clearing one does not clear the rest, so check the ride the child actually wants. Splash Academy runs Turtles 3–5, Seals 6–9 and Dolphins 10–12, with Entourage for teens 13–17. Guppies covers 6 months to 2 years but it's a parent-participation play session, not drop-off childcare — don't let a couple plan an evening around it. Core programming is free; the Late Night Fun Zone is $10 an hour per child. Registration is a one-time form per child, done on embarkation day. A tall six-year-old still gets turned away at the slide.
traps.flag[1]: If you've booked a balcony, confirm the view isn't blocked. The documented issue on this class is not a blocked view at all — it's the slide structure running down the hull past the balconies between decks 8 and 16, entering the balcony on some cabins. Treat that as a geometry check on the specific room. Lists of specific cabin numbers circulate, but they come from a single site that concedes in the same article that NCL doesn't flag most of them, so none of those numbers are repeated here. What's actually in the way matters here: the ship's dry-slide structure running down the side of the hull, physically entering the balcony — this one is not a view problem and calling it "obstructed" misses it entirely — the client still has a balcony and the sea is still there, but the slide structure comes INTO the balcony space rather than passing outside it. The rooms with the biggest balconies are the ones reported worst affected, which is the opposite of what anyone expects. Describe the geometry; don't file it under obstructed and let them imagine a wall. The deck plan doesn't always flag it, and an obstructed view is the first thing the client notices.
traps.flag[2]: Nothing sits underneath the go-kart track. The Speedway runs across decks 18 to 20 and what's directly below it is the deck 17 pool deck, not staterooms — the nearest cabins are two decks further down. If a client has been warned off this ship over kart noise in the cabin, the deck plan doesn't support it, and correcting that is worth as much as finding a bad cabin.
traps.flag[3]: Ocean Boulevard, the wraparound promenade on deck 8, has no cabins on it. This is NOT Royal Promenade geometry — there's no corridor of stateroom windows looking onto a public walkway, so none of the privacy problems you'd warn about on those ships apply here. traps.why: Every line splits kids' programming and thrill rides by age and height, and the cutoffs aren't on the booking page. A parent who was promised the waterpark and gets a crying kid at the rope is a parent who books with someone else next year.
traps.linePolicy[0]: Be precise about The Haven, because two different mistakes cost bookings. traps.linePolicy[1]: Freestyle means no assigned table and no fixed dinner time, which is the selling point — but it also means everyone turns up at once. The 6:30 to 7:30 window fills hard on the bigger ships and queueing is routine. Tell them to eat at 5:30 or after 8, or to book ahead even where it isn't required. The ships show colour-coded capacity boards for each venue; a red bar means don't walk over.
traps.linePolicy[2]: Prepaid service charges do not cover bar, beverage or specialty-dining gratuities. That one sentence causes more onboard disputes than anything else on this line — say it at final payment.
traps.linePolicy[3]: Free at Sea Plus is $49.99 per person per day, applies to guests one and two, and every guest in the stateroom has to take the same offer. It has to be added at least 72 hours before sailing and can't be changed onboard, so it's a pre-cruise decision or it's nothing.
traps.linePolicy[4]: Drinks at Great Stirrup Cay, the private island, are carved out of standard Free at Sea and sold as a separate island package. Free at Sea Plus covers them; the standard bundle doesn't. Clients assume the private island is included and it isn't.
traps.linePolicy[5]: Wi-Fi is per device per day — around $30 for browsing and $40 for streaming. A couple with two phones each is paying four times what they think they are.
traps.linePolicy[6]: Room service carries a convenience fee per order, about $5 at breakfast and up to $10 the rest of the day. It's waived in suites and The Haven, so a client moving down from a suite next time will notice.

A Haven couple on a week is around $53.50 each per day before they buy a thing. Two more catches: the specialty dining in the bundle goes to guests one and two only, and a second guest under 21 gets a soda package at $12.50 a day charged separately, while guests three and up under 21 get no substitute at all.
money.flag[1]: Book specialty dining now, before they board. Book at 120 days out, the moment it opens — and know you're already behind. Suites, Club Balcony and the top Latitudes tiers get in at 125 days and clear the 6:30 to 8:00 slots at Cagney's, Le Bistro and Ocean Blue before general booking even starts. Take 5:30 or 9:00 rather than nothing, and warn them the "free" dinner still surcharges lobster and the premium steak cuts, with a second main at $25. When the client can't get a table they blame you, not the ship.
money.why: A drink package has to be consumed on the ship. When the itinerary pulls them ashore five days out of seven, the daily rate almost never breaks even. Sell it and they feel it was a waste — and they remember who suggested it.
traps.verified: true
traps.call: Watch the walking. This is a big ship, and the distance from a far cabin to the theater or dining room is longer than anyone expects — it wears on older travelers by day three.
traps.flag[0]: Map their daily route before you book the cabin. I'm deliberately giving you less here than an earlier version of this record did, and the reason matters. That version warned there was no midship lift bank, that the banks sat at dead ends, and that there's no continuous fore-and-aft interior corridor — the strongest accessibility warning in this whole database, resting on ambiguous deck-plan reading. None of it is confirmed, and a wrong mobility recommendation is the most expensive kind to get wrong. So: the lift bank layout is UNCHARTED here. Map the actual route from the specific cabin to the dining room and the theatre before you commit, and confirm it against NCL's accessible deck plan rather than against any rule I could give you. A great-looking aft suite can mean a punishing walk to everything, every night.
traps.flag[1]: If you've booked a balcony, confirm the view isn't blocked. The documented issue on this class is not a blocked view at all — it's the slide structure running down the hull past the balconies between decks 8 and 16, entering the balcony on some cabins. Treat that as a geometry check on the specific room. Beyond it, NCL doesn't publish a full obstructed list and says so obliquely in its own guarantee terms, which warn that a guarantee balcony may be fully or partially obstructed. Lists of specific cabin numbers circulate, but they come from a single site that concedes in the same article that NCL doesn't flag most of them, so none of those numbers are repeated here. What's actually in the way matters here: the ship's dry-slide structure running down the side of the hull, physically entering the balcony — this one is not a view problem and calling it "obstructed" misses it entirely — the client still has a balcony and the sea is still there, but the slide structure comes INTO the balcony space rather than passing outside it. The rooms with the biggest balconies are the ones reported worst affected, which is the opposite of what anyone expects. Describe the geometry; don't file it under obstructed and let them imagine a wall. The deck plan doesn't always flag it, and an obstructed view is the first thing the client notices.
traps.flag[2]: Nothing sits underneath the go-kart track. The Speedway runs across decks 18 to 20 and what's directly below it is the deck 17 pool deck, not staterooms — the nearest cabins are two decks further down. If a client has been warned off this ship over kart noise in the cabin, the deck plan doesn't support it, and correcting that is worth as much as finding a bad cabin.
traps.flag[3]: Ocean Boulevard, the wraparound promenade on deck 8, has no cabins on it. This is NOT Royal Promenade geometry — there's no corridor of stateroom windows looking onto a public walkway, so none of the privacy problems you'd warn about on those ships apply here.
